evidence_set: Compared with continuing to smoke, stopping at 25 to 34 (median 29) gave survival nearly the same as never smoking, about 10 years of life gained; at 35 to 44 (median 39) about 9 years, with a hazard ratio of 1.2 against people who never smoked, against 3.0 in the text for people who continued (excess cut by about 90%); at 45 to 54 about 6 years, excess cut by about two thirds; at 55 to 64 about 4 years. The text cites Figure 4 for the ratios of 1.2 and 3.0, but the figure prints 2.9 (99% CI 2.7 to 3.1) for continued smoking and 1.2 (1.0 to 1.4) for stopping at 35 to 44; the ratios for the other ages at stopping are shown there and in the Supplementary Appendix (not opened) and are not used here. People may have stopped because of illness, which would overstate the risk in the group that stopped; leaving out the first 2 years of follow-up left the results similar (data not shown).

How the report's judgments are made: four levels (sufficient to infer a causal relationship; suggestive but not sufficient; inadequate to infer the presence or absence of a causal relationship; suggestive of no causal relationship) from a synthesis of all the evidence on consistency, strength, specificity, temporality and coherence; chapters written by 75 experts and reviewed by more than 100 peer reviewers; chapters 1 and 3 state no databases, dates or selection rules for the evidence behind the conclusions (chapter 3 says each section's author assembles all of the relevant evidence available; the chapters that hold the conclusions used here were not read), so the report is read as a narrative review.

evidence_set: The six graded conclusions of the nicotine chapter: sufficient to infer that at high enough doses nicotine has acute toxicity (1); that nicotine activates multiple biological pathways through which smoking increases the risk of disease (2); that nicotine exposure during fetal development has lasting adverse consequences for brain development (3); that nicotine adversely affects maternal and fetal health in pregnancy, contributing to adverse outcomes such as preterm delivery and stillbirth (4). Suggestive (the chapter's word; level 2 of the report's scale, 'suggestive but not sufficient') that exposure during adolescence may have lasting adverse consequences for brain development (5). Inadequate to infer the presence or absence of a causal relationship between nicotine and cancer risk (6).

Acute toxicity data on nicotine are limited and come from three sources: animal studies, trials of nicotine as a medicine and poisoning reports. The animal studies do not adequately characterize acute toxicity; the medicine trials use amounts chosen, in part, because they are thought to be subtoxic; poisonings are documented, but it appears that the literature has not been assessed systematically for the relation between amount and effect; the commonly quoted human fatal oral amount is poorly documented (the chapter's literature search found no source for it). The Summary says nicotine has known acute toxicity and that poisoning is possible from ingesting nicotine-containing products. No amounts are used in this claim.

Inference about nicotine alone in pregnancy comes from studies comparing prenatal smokeless tobacco with prenatal smoking (smokeless products do not expose people to combustion products but all contain nicotine; Swedish snus has lower levels of certain toxicants than conventional smokeless products) and from randomized trials of nicotine therapy in pregnant women. Fetal growth: smokeless tobacco shows only modest contributions to lower birth weight; Swedish population study 1999 to 2010, snus and small-for-gestational-age term births, adjusted odds ratio 1.21 (95% CI 1.02 to 1.43), smaller than for smoking (the smoking figure is printed as 2.27 with an interval of 2.62 to 2.91, so it is not quoted); a trial of 250 pregnant women found no difference in quit rates or saliva cotinine between nicotine-patch and placebo arms but a birth weight 186 g higher (35 to 336) in the patch arm, possibly due to less smoking; the chapter reads these as supporting a modest role for nicotine in fetal growth restriction. Preterm delivery: smoking linked to a 27% higher risk (Shah and Bracken 2000, as cited); rises of similar size with snus and with smoking in Sweden. Stillbirth: higher risk with smokeless tobacco in India and Sweden; in the Swedish study the smoking-related stillbirth risk fell markedly when antenatal bleeding and small-for-gestational-age deliveries were excluded while the snus risk stayed the same, which the chapter reads as both involving nicotine, with other factors possibly also contributing in smoking. Summary: the evidence supports the hypothesis that nicotine plays a key role in mediating the adverse effects of smoking on reproductive health, including preterm delivery and stillbirth.

Genotoxicity data are mixed (most studies negative; five positive: two for chromosomal aberration and sister chromatid exchange, and one each for micronuclei, an E. coli mutation assay and the Comet assay in nasal cells; DNA adducts also reported). Animal studies mostly do not show nicotine alone to be tumour-causing (one exception: sarcomas in one mouse strain); nicotine promotes tumours in some models but not those driven by tobacco-specific nitrosamines; the animal findings do not support nicotine as a complete carcinogen. People: very little data; the Lung Health Study is the only source on long-term nicotine replacement (5,887 enrolled, 3,220 followed 7 more years, 75 lung cancers, no link with replacement use; short follow-up); smokeless tobacco raises the risk of cancers of the mouth, oesophagus and pancreas (at least for some forms), less than smoking, and does not raise many smoking-related cancers, which suggests nicotine may not have a strong tumour-promoting effect, tempered by the different route (oral rather than inhaled). Summary: insufficient data to conclude that nicotine causes or contributes to cancer in humans; possible oral, oesophageal and pancreatic risks; substantial experimental evidence that nicotine is active in carcinogenic mechanisms; in vitro data suggestive but not supported overall by the most recent animal studies.

Grading in the report: four levels from a synthesis of all the evidence, using consistency, strength, specificity, temporality and coherence; meta-analytic significance has not figured directly in its causal inferences; conclusions are worded conservatively; chapters 1 and 3 describe no databases, dates or selection rules for the conclusions used (chapter 5 names one search, in OVID MEDLINE, the Hazardous Substances Data Bank and Haz-Map, for a source of the commonly quoted human fatal oral amount, gives no dates, and found none), so the report is read as a narrative review.

evidence_set: Conclusions bearing on a lowest safe level (the editors' reading; chapter 1 does not link them to the statement, and chapter 2 was not read): more than 50 carcinogens in sidestream and secondhand smoke (1); sufficient that secondhand smoke and its condensates cause tumours in laboratory animals (2); sufficient that exposure of people who do not smoke raises urinary levels of metabolites of a tobacco-specific lung carcinogen (3); the mechanisms of lung cancer are probably similar to those in people who smoke, with the overall risk compared with active smoking diminished by a substantially lower carcinogenic dose (4); multiple mechanisms of respiratory tract injury (5) and mechanisms by which secondhand smoke could raise the risk of sudden infant death syndrome (6); sufficient: a clot-promoting effect (7), dysfunction of the cells lining blood vessels (8) and atherosclerosis in animal models (9).

Reproductive and developmental effects, graded by the 2006 report. Sufficient to infer a causal relationship: sudden infant death syndrome (4) and a small reduction in birth weight from maternal exposure in pregnancy (6). Suggestive but not sufficient: preterm delivery (5) and childhood cancer overall with exposure before and after birth (11), leukaemias (14), lymphomas (15) and brain tumours (16). Inadequate to infer the presence or absence of a causal relationship: female fertility (1), spontaneous abortion (2), neonatal mortality (3), congenital malformations (7), cognitive functioning (8), behavioural problems (9), height and growth (10), childhood cancer from maternal exposure in pregnancy (12) or exposure in infancy (13), and other childhood cancers (17). Chapter 1 gives no relative risks for these.

Respiratory effects in children (the exposure in conclusions 1 and 3 to 10 is parental smoking). Sufficient: lower respiratory illnesses in infants and children (1), with the greatest increase in risk from the mother's smoking (2); middle ear disease (3); cough, phlegm, wheeze and breathlessness (6) and ever having asthma (7) at school age; onset of wheeze illnesses in early childhood (8); persistent adverse effects on lung function across childhood from the mother's smoking in pregnancy (11); lower lung function in childhood from exposure after birth (12). Suggestive but not sufficient: natural history of middle ear effusion (4) and onset of childhood asthma (9). Inadequate: adenoidectomy or tonsillectomy (5) and immunoglobulin E-mediated allergy (10).

Heart and blood vessels. Sufficient: coronary heart disease morbidity and mortality in men and women (1), with pooled relative risks from meta-analyses indicating a 25 to 30 percent increase in risk (2). Suggestive but not sufficient: stroke (3), and studies of subclinical vascular disease, particularly thickening of the carotid artery wall, as a basis for inferring a causal relationship with atherosclerosis (4).

Respiratory effects in adults. Sufficient: odour annoyance (1) and nasal irritation (2). Suggestive but not sufficient: greater susceptibility to nasal irritation in people with nasal allergies or a history of respiratory illnesses (3), acute respiratory symptoms in people with asthma (4) and in healthy people (5), chronic respiratory symptoms (6), short-term decline in lung function in people with asthma (7), a small decrement in lung function from chronic exposure (9), adult-onset asthma (11), worsening of asthma control (12) and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (13). Inadequate: short-term lung function decline in healthy people (8), accelerated decline in lung function (10) and morbidity in people with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (14).

Random misclassification of exposure tends to reduce the apparent effect; classifying some people who currently or formerly smoked as people who never smoked would tend to push the lung cancer association upward when smoking clusters between spouses, but the analyses cited cannot fully explain the observed increase this way; because exposure has been widespread and almost unavoidable there are no truly unexposed persons, so estimates may be biased downward. Meta-analysis is used with the recognition that the uncertainty around pooled estimates may exceed what conventional statistics show, because of biases in or selection of the studies; one analysis of 37 studies suggested that smaller studies gave higher risks, another found little evidence of publication bias, and efforts to find possibly missing studies are said to have yielded little or nothing that would alter published conclusions (the printed sentence is garbled); the pooled results were not decisive for the causal conclusions. Confounding: adults with more exposure tend to have less healthful lifestyles in US and UK surveys (how far this generalizes is uncertain), socioeconomic status may lie on the causal pathway, and confounding matters more as associations get weaker.

Process and grading: 22 experts wrote initial chapters, consolidated into 10, reviewed by more than 40 peer reviewers and more than 30 scientists for scientific integrity, then by agencies of the US Department of Health and Human Services; the same four levels as in the 2014 report, with consistency, strength, specificity (set aside as not relevant), temporality and coherence used as guidelines and not as a checklist; a small elevation of risk does not weigh against causality but alternative explanations need full exploration, and, from knowledge of dosimetry and mechanisms, the risk is anticipated to be only slightly or modestly raised for some associations such as lung cancer, particularly when the very strong relative risks found for active smokers are compared with those for lifetime nonsmokers; reviews cover evidence identified through search strategies set out in each chapter (not read), mechanisms evidence was selectively reviewed, and newer key references are listed in an appendix.

The report says the tobacco industry has criticized the evidence repeatedly, funded or carried out research judged to be biased and tried to undermine key studies and sustain controversy; it identifies industry sponsorship of publications only where relevant to interpretation, and notes that papers acknowledging industry support addressed the lung cancer findings (study selection and quality, meta-analysis methods, dose-response associations) amid focused criticisms of the use of meta-analysis.

Grading in the 2014 report: four levels from a synthesis of all the evidence; meta-analytic significance has not figured directly in its causal inferences; chapters 1 and 3 describe no databases, dates or selection rules for the conclusions (chapter 8, which holds the conclusions used here, was not read), so the report is read as a narrative review.

evidence_set: PubMed (100 records), EMBASE (207) and Web of Science (92), 246 after removing duplicates; two reviewers worked independently at each stage; 227 excluded (108 reported no mortality by cigar use, 90 non-epidemiologic or non-human, 13 non-English, 7 repeated results from included cohorts, 3 unpublished abstracts, 2 on causes not on the lists, 2 with former or current cigarette smokers in the reference group, 2 an earlier study of lifetime ever-use) and 3 added by handsearching: 22 articles from 16 prospective cohorts (12 US, 5 UK, 1 Canada, 4 Nordic papers), beginning between the 1940s and the 1980s; CPS-I 15,191 and CPS-II 7,888 primary cigar smokers (current, exclusive cigar smoking with no previous cigarette or pipe smoking); CPS-II had no women because they were not asked about cigars. No protocol or registration is mentioned.

The main exposure is current exclusive cigar smoking (or cigar and/or pipe); people who currently smoke cigarettes are excluded so as to isolate cigars; 'primary' means no history of cigarette or pipe smoking and 'secondary' means such a history; in CPS-I people in the secondary group were about twice as likely as those in the primary group to report inhaling (42.0% against 21.6%); the reference group is people who never smoked or never used tobacco; results are given descriptively as 'mortality ratios' (standardized mortality ratios, hazard ratios, incidence rate ratios and odds ratios, some calculated by the reviewers) because exposure definitions, dose categories and adjustment vary.

Primary cigar smoking, CPS-I / CPS-II: oral 7.92 (5.12 to 11.69) / 4.0 (1.5 to 10.3); oesophageal 3.60 (2.17 to 5.62) / 1.8 (0.9 to 3.7); laryngeal 10.02 (4.01 to 20.64) / 10.3 (2.6 to 41.0); the Dorn study (current cigar smoking whatever the earlier cigarette history) gives 4.11, 10.33 for oral and laryngeal cancer, in the same direction. Oral cancer by cigars a day in CPS-I 2.12 (0.43 to 6.18), 8.51 and 15.94; oesophageal ratios are flat across amount and inhalation in CPS-II. No inhalation reported: oral 6.98 (4.13 to 11.03) and 3.2 (0.9 to 11.0); oesophageal 3.4 (1.90 to 5.61) and 1.6 (0.7 to 4.1); laryngeal 10.6 (3.87 to 23.07) and 4.2 (0.5 to 37.1). Small numbers at 1 to 2 cigars a day leave intervals that include 1 (oral cancer in CPS-II could not be estimated: no exposed cases).

Primary cigar smoking, CPS-I / CPS-II: pancreatic cancer 1.62 (1.22 to 2.11) / 1.3 (0.9 to 1.9); bladder cancer 1.38 (0.89 to 2.04) / 1.0 (0.4 to 2.3); coronary heart disease 1.05 (1.00 to 1.11) / 1.30 (1.05 to 1.62) in men 30 to 74 and 0.93 (0.72 to 1.21) at 75 and over; stroke 0.96 (0.87 to 1.06) in CPS-I; aortic aneurysm 1.76 (1.29 to 2.35) in CPS-I; chronic obstructive pulmonary disease 1.42 (0.96 to 2.03) primary and 4.39 (3.02 to 6.16) secondary in CPS-I. Primary cigar and/or pipe smoking and coronary heart disease 0.98 (0.67 to 1.44) in the Wald cohort. Coronary heart disease gradients with amount and inhalation are weak, among primary but not secondary cigar smokers in CPS-I.

The authors prioritize primary cigar smoking in the larger cohorts. Outcomes significantly associated with primary cigar smoking in one or both CPS cohorts: all causes, oral, oesophageal, pancreatic, laryngeal and lung cancers, coronary heart disease and aortic aneurysm; dose trends for the four cancers; raised risks of oral, oesophageal and laryngeal cancer with no inhalation, particularly in CPS-I, which they say is consistent with cigar smoke being inhaled regardless of self-report (one cited study); raised but mostly non-significant ratios at 1 to 2 cigars a day for those three cancers and aortic aneurysm. In CPS-I the risks were considerably higher for secondary than for primary cigar smoking for lung cancer (6.29 against 2.1) and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (4.39 against 1.42), which they say could be due to different inhalation and could also be explained by lung damage from earlier cigarette smoking.

As cited by the review and not re-read: the International Agency for Research on Cancer concluded in 2004 that cigar and/or pipe smoking causes cancers of the lung and upper aerodigestive tract and found evidence that it is causally associated with cancers of the pancreas, stomach and bladder. In the EPIC cohort (incident cancers, median follow-up 9 years), 1,451 people had smoked only cigars (74% currently, 26% formerly); among those currently smoking only cigars the hazard ratio was 3.9 for lung cancer and 3.5 for upper aerodigestive tract cancer, the hazard ratio for any tobacco-related cancer was 1.6 and a significantly raised risk of any tobacco-related cancer was still seen when no inhalation was reported (the review gives no figure for it), and the combined risk of lung, upper aerodigestive tract and bladder cancers rose with cigars a day and was raised across small, medium and large cigars. In an INHANCE pooled analysis of 19 studies (13,935 cases and 18,691 controls), people who never smoked cigarettes but ever smoked cigars had an odds ratio of 2.54 (95% CI 1.93 to 3.34) for head and neck cancer, rising with frequency and duration, while the ratio was not raised among people who had ever smoked cigarettes.
